opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. Honestly, a big part of it comes down to efficiency and sustainability, which is what I spend most of my time thinking about. Right now there's this trend of taking huge, general-purpose generative models and using them for everything, even really simple tasks like classifying sentiment or answering a factual question. When we actually measured this, comparing task-specific models with multi-purpose generative models on the same tasks, the general-purpose ones used dramatically more energy. Often it was orders of magnitude more, and they didn't necessarily perform better. So you're paying a big environmental and financial cost for flexibility you don't actually need.

Beyond energy, there's a practical side. When you deploy AI in the real world, you usually have a specific problem: a hospital triaging images, a company routing customer emails, a researcher detecting species from camera traps. A smaller model trained or fine-tuned for that context is easier to evaluate. You know what "good" looks like, and you can test it against the data it will actually see. With a giant general model, it's much harder to characterize its failure modes, because it can do a million things and you can't test them all.

There's also transparency and control. Smaller, specialized models are often open, can run locally, and can be audited. Communities can adapt them to their language or their domain instead of depending on a handful of companies with massive compute. That matters for data privacy, for cost, and frankly for who gets to participate in AI.

So it's not that general models are useless. They're great for exploration and for genuinely open-ended tasks. But I'd love for people to ask, "What's the right tool for this job?" instead of defaulting to the biggest hammer available. Very often, the right tool is smaller, cheaper, greener, and works just as well or better in context.

r001.rationale: It says general-purpose models are often used for simple tasks and that a smaller model suited to the specific problem can work as well or better.

r002.rationale: It does not describe classifying a query's intent and using that classification to choose a model.

r003.rationale: It does not mention mixture-of-experts models or connect them to routing queries among selected models.

r004.rationale: It says general models are harder to evaluate and characterize, but does not state that models cannot be good at all possible tasks.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so this is something I've been thinking about for a long time, and it really comes back to a few things. The first is efficiency. When you look at what people are actually doing with AI in the real world, a lot of it is pretty narrow tasks: classifying documents, extracting information, summarizing text, answering questions about a specific domain. And for those tasks, a lot of the work I've done with colleagues has shown that a smaller model that's been fine-tuned for that task will often perform just as well, sometimes better, than a huge general-purpose model, while using a fraction of the energy and compute.

I did a study a couple of years ago where we compared models across different tasks, and the difference between a task-specific model and a general-purpose multi-task model for something like question answering or classification was something like twenty or thirty times more energy for the general-purpose one. And that's per query. When you multiply that by millions or billions of queries a day, it really adds up. So from a sustainability perspective, it's hard to justify using a model that can write poetry and generate code when all you need it to do is tell you whether an email is spam.

The second piece is about control and understanding. With a task-specific model, you know what data went into it, you can evaluate it properly on the task you care about, and you can actually reason about failure modes. With these massive general-purpose models, you often don't know what's in the training data, the evaluation is this moving target of benchmarks that may or may not reflect your use case, and you get these emergent behaviors that nobody really planned for. In a deployment context, especially in high-stakes settings like healthcare or hiring or legal, that opacity is a real problem.

And then the third thing, which I think is underappreciated, is that context matters enormously. A model that works well in one language, one culture, one domain, won't necessarily transfer. So the idea that we're going to have one model that does everything for everyone everywhere, I find that both technically dubious and kind of philosophically questionable. I'd much rather see an ecosystem of smaller, well-documented, purpose-built models that communities can actually adapt and own, than this concentration of everything into a handful of giant systems that only a few companies can train. That's not to say general-purpose models have no place, but I think the default should be "what's the smallest, most appropriate tool for this job," not "let's throw the biggest model we can find at it."

r001.rationale: The response says many real-world tasks are narrow and that smaller task-specific models can perform as well as or better than huge general-purpose models.

r003.rationale: It does not mention mixture-of-experts models or connect them to routing queries among selected models.

r004.rationale: It argues that a model that works well in one language, culture, or domain may not transfer, and calls the idea of one model doing everything technically dubious.

astra-6.text:
Because in most real-world applications, you have a particular problem you’re trying to solve. If you want to classify a document or identify something in an image, you don’t necessarily need a model that can also write poetry and generate code. You need something that does that task well.

A more specialized model can be smaller, use less energy, and be easier to evaluate. You can ask, does it work for this language, for this domain, for the people who are actually going to use it? A model’s performance on a broad benchmark doesn’t necessarily tell you that.

There’s a place for general-purpose models, especially when you’re exploring what’s possible. But once you know what you need, I think it makes sense to choose a model that fits those needs, rather than assuming the biggest model is always the best choice.

sol-6.1.text:
I think we should start with the task and ask what kind of model we actually need to solve it. If you’re classifying documents or identifying something in an image, you don’t necessarily need a general-purpose model that can also write poetry and generate code. A smaller, task-specific model can be very effective, and it can use fewer computational resources.

There’s also the question of evaluating it. When you have a clearly defined task and context, you can test whether the model does what you need it to do, understand where it fails, and decide whether those failures are acceptable for that application. With a model that’s supposed to do everything, that becomes much harder.

So for me, it’s about matching the tool to the problem. General-purpose models have useful applications, but they shouldn’t automatically be the starting point for every problem.
